label: Philippians 1:1
text:
Paul and Timothy call themselves *douloi* (δοῦλοι), bondslaves — the word for someone born into slavery, bound to a master by a tie only death can break, with no will left but the master's.

There is no article in the Greek: not "the servants" but servants by nature, by category of being.

"Timothy" is built from two Greek roots meaning roughly "one who honors God" — a name the man grew into.

The recipients are *hagioi* (ἅγιοι), "set-apart ones" — the same root gives us saint, sanctify, holy. Pagan Greeks used this verb of consecrating a building as a temple; Paul applies it to people, set apart from sin for God's use.

"In Christ Jesus" is a locative of sphere — Christ is the space believers now live inside, the way a temple precinct marks off consecrated ground.

"Bishop" (*episkopos*, ἐπίσκοπος) literally means "one who looks upon, an overseer," a term borrowed from secular project-oversight.

"Deacon" (*diakonos*, διάκονος) is the ordinary word for a servant defined by activity rather than status — the same word rendered "minister" elsewhere in Paul.
translation: Paul and Timothy, bondslaves belonging to Christ Jesus, to all the set-apart ones in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, together with the overseers and servants.

label: Philippians 1:2
text:
*Charis* (χάρις), "grace," named among the Greeks a favor granted freely, with no expectation of repayment — but always from one friend to another.

Paul stretches the word past its ordinary reach: God's favor at the cross went out to His enemies, not His friends, which was unheard of in the word's normal use. *Eirēnē* (εἰρήνη), "peace," carries an older sense of "binding together" — not simply an absence of conflict but a knitting of two parties, God and the believer, into one relationship.
translation: Grace to you, and peace, from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

label: Philippians 1:5
text:
*Koinōnia* (κοινωνία), "fellowship," meant a joint-participation in a shared undertaking, not mere companionship — here, the Philippians' shared stake with Paul in spreading the gospel, from their first support of him up to the present.

One small, telling detail: the Greek puts a definite article before "now" — literally "until the now" — a quiet pointer to the specific gift Epaphroditus had just delivered, which Paul is too tactful to name outright so soon.
translation: I am continually thanking my God over your joint-participation in the gospel, from the first day until the this-present-moment.

label: Philippians 1:6
text:
"Being confident" carries a causal edge in the Greek — Paul's thanksgiving flows out of a settled conviction, not a passing hope. The verb is the one used for having been fully persuaded: Paul has weighed the matter and reached a fixed conclusion that God, who started the work in them, will carry it through to completion.

"Until the day of Christ Jesus" treats that day as near at hand, close enough to shape present confidence.
translation: Being one who has come to this settled persuasion, that he who began a good work in you will keep on completing it, right up to the day of Christ Jesus.

label: Philippians 1:7
text:
Paul says it is only "right" — a word meaning "just," not merely fitting — to feel this way about them.

His "thinking" is the kind that keeps turning practically toward someone's good, not idle sentiment.

"Defense" translates *apologia* (ἀπολογία), a courtroom term for the speech an advocate makes on a defendant's behalf; Paul pictures himself defending the gospel before Rome's own tribunal.

And grammatically "my" belongs with "partakers," not "grace": the Philippians are Paul's co-sharers in this grace, partners with him specifically, not simply recipients of a grace that happens to be his.
translation: Even as it is right for me to be thinking this concerning all of you, because you are holding me in your heart, both in my bonds and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel, you all being fellow-partakers with me of the grace.

label: Philippians 1:8
text:
"Record" translates *martys* (μάρτυς), "witness" — the very word behind "martyr." Paul calls God to testify, something he does only in his most solemn moments.

"Long after" is *epipotheō* (ἐπιποθέω), the ordinary word for desire strengthened by an intensifying prefix — a straining, earnest longing.

He locates that longing not in his own heart but "in the bowels of Christ Jesus" — the upper organs the ancients regarded as the seat of tender affection, what we would call the heart. Paul's longing for the Philippians is described less as his own emotion than as Christ's affection operating through him.
translation: For God is my witness, how I am continually longing after all of you with the tender affections of Christ Jesus.

label: Philippians 1:9–11
text:
"Pray" is *proseuchomai* (προσεύχομαι), prayer consciously addressed to a listening Person, not words tossed into the air.

Paul asks that their love "abound" — *perisseuō* (περισσεύω), to exceed the ordinary measure, to run over.

But an overflow needs banks: "knowledge" is *epignōsis* (ἐπίγνωσις), full, experiential knowledge rather than mere information, and "judgment" translates a word for trained, sensitive moral tact — the discernment to say and do the right thing, not just mean well.

"Approve" is *dokimazō* (δοκιμάζω), to test something and then certify it genuine — the word used of examiners passing a candidate.

What they are to test and approve are "the things that differ," a phrase built on a verb meaning "to carry in different directions" — the finer distinctions of conduct, not the obvious moral basics.

The goal is to be *eilikrinēs* (εἰλικρινής), unmixed and pure, and *aproskopos* (ἀπρόσκοπος), literally "not stumbled against" — giving no one else occasion to trip.
translation: And this is what I am continually praying, that your love may keep on overflowing still more and more, in full experiential knowledge and all moral tact, so that you may test and approve the things that differ, in order that you may be pure and giving no one occasion to stumble, until the day of Christ, having been filled to the full with the fruit of righteousness which comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

label: Philippians 1:12
text:
"Understand" translates a verb for knowledge gained through experience, not secondhand report — Paul wants the Philippians to learn something by watching what has happened to him.

"The things concerning me" is literally "the things dominating me" in Greek — his circumstances are not background noise but the ruling fact of his present life.

"Furtherance" is *prokopē* (προκοπή), built on a verb meaning "to cut in front of" — used of the pioneer crew of woodcutters who hacked a road through forest ahead of an advancing army. Paul's imprisonment has not merely failed to stop the gospel; it has cut fresh road for it into ground the message could not otherwise have reached.
translation: Now I want you to know, brothers, that the things concerning me have come to result rather in the pioneer-advance of the gospel.

label: Philippians 1:13
text:
"Manifest" translates a phrase meaning "have become plainly known" — the reason for Paul's imprisonment worked its way through the ranks by word of mouth until it was common knowledge.

"Palace" renders *praitōrion* (πραιτώριον), the Praetorian Guard — the elite imperial regiments whose barracks held Paul's rotating chain of guards. Each soldier who took his shift heard the gospel firsthand, chained wrist to wrist with the apostle for hours at a stretch.
translation: So that my bonds have become plainly known to be in Christ, throughout the whole Praetorian Guard and to all the rest.

label: Philippians 1:14
text:
"Many" is literally "the majority" — most, not all, of the believers in Rome had found new nerve to preach.

"Waxing confident" comes from a verb meaning "to persuade": watching Paul's fearlessness in chains had persuaded them into a settled boldness "in the Lord." But two very different motives divided these preachers. Some spoke out of *eritheia* (ἐριθεία), factious self-seeking — a term for the hired partisan spirit of a political operator — hoping to needle Paul's chains with jealousy.

Others preached from simple goodwill, knowing Paul was "set" — literally "appointed" — to the defense of the gospel, wanting to lighten, not sharpen, his burden.
translation: And the majority of the brothers, having been persuaded by my bonds, are becoming confident in the Lord to speak the word without fear, more abundantly than before. Some indeed are proclaiming Christ even out of envy and factious self-seeking, but others out of goodwill — these out of love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel, but those out of a partisan spirit, insincerely, thinking to stir up trouble for me in my bonds.

label: Philippians 1:18
text:
Whatever the motive, Paul asks simply, "What is my feeling about it?" and answers that Christ is being proclaimed either way — enough to make him rejoice.

He then turns to his own outcome, using *sōtēria* (σωτηρία), "salvation," in its broader sense of deliverance or well-being, not only eternal rescue.

"Earnest expectation" is *apokaradokia* (ἀποκαραδοκία), a compound built on "head" and "to watch," picturing someone straining forward with head outstretched, eyes fixed on one point — the classic image is a watchman scanning the horizon for a signal-beacon.

"Boldness" is *parrēsia* (παρρησία), literally "all-speech" or free speech — courage that holds nothing back.

Paul's hope is that Christ will be "magnified," *megalynō* (μεγαλύνω), made great and conspicuous, in his body whether he lives or dies.
translation: Now what is my feeling? Only this: that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is being proclaimed, and in this I rejoice — yes, and I will keep on rejoicing. For I know that this will turn out for my deliverance, through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, according to my straining expectation and hope, that in nothing I shall be put to shame, but that with all boldness of speech, as always, so now, Christ shall be made conspicuous in my body, whether through life or through death.

label: Philippians 1:21
text:
"For me to live is Christ" — Christ is not a cause Paul serves from outside but the very sphere his existence operates within, an energizing Person animating his life from the inside.

The infinitive translated "to die" is better rendered "to have died" — the tense points not to the act of dying but to the resulting state afterward. Death holds no sting for Paul precisely because what lies on the other side of it, not the act itself, is what he calls gain.
translation: For to me, to be living — that is Christ, and to have died is gain.

label: Philippians 1:22
text:
The strait Paul describes — hemmed in from both sides — uses a definite article in Greek before "two," pointing back to the two options just named, life and death, each pulling with equal weight and holding him motionless between them.

"Desire" is a strengthened word for passionate longing, not a mild preference.

"To depart" translates *analyō* (ἀναλύω), used of a ship slipping its moorings or a soldier striking his tent — fitting language from a man who made tents for a living and was, at that moment, a prisoner in a military camp.

"To abide in the flesh" pictures clinging to this present, inconvenient body rather than simply "continuing to live."
translation: But if to go on living in the flesh — this is the fruit of my labor, then I do not know what to choose. But I am hemmed in from both sides by the two, having the passionate desire to strike my tent and be with Christ, which is far better; yet to remain on in the flesh is more necessary for your sake.

label: Philippians 1:25
text:
"Confidence" sits in the perfect tense — a settled conviction reached only after Paul turned the matter over fully in his mind, not a snap feeling. Having weighed it, he concludes the Philippians need his ministry more than he needs to depart.

"Continue" carries the specific sense of remaining alive, and "furtherance" is the same word rendered earlier as "pioneer-advance" — Paul expects to go on cutting fresh road into their spiritual progress.
translation: And having come to this settled conviction, I know that I shall remain and continue on with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith.

label: Philippians 1:26
text: "Coming" translates *parousia* (παρουσία), literally "being alongside" — the same word used elsewhere of Christ's own return, His personal presence among His people. Paul's promised visit to Philippi is described in the vocabulary usually reserved for the Lord's own arrival; his presence there will be the occasion, not merely the announcement, of their increased joy.
translation: So that your rejoicing may keep overflowing in Christ Jesus because of me, through my coming to be present with you again.

label: Philippians 1:27
text:
The word behind "let your conversation be" is not the ordinary word for conduct but *politeuomai* (πολιτεύομαι), built on the word for a city and its citizen body — the verb for discharging the duties owed by a member of a political community to its whole and its head. Philippi was a Roman colony proud of its citizenship, and Paul reaches for a word his readers would recognize instantly: live as citizens, discharging your obligations to your commonwealth — except here the commonwealth is heaven. The verb is middle voice, meaning the subject acts on itself: the saints are to hold themselves to this standard, not merely be held to it by another.

"Becometh" translates a word meaning literally "weighing as much as" — their manner of life is to carry the same weight as the gospel they claim to believe, so their words are not emptied of substance by a mismatched life.
translation: Only, be discharging your citizen-duty in a manner that weighs as much as the gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may keep hearing about you — that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one soul contending together as a team for the faith of the gospel.

label: Philippians 1:28
text:
"Terrified" pictures the fright of a startled horse, a sudden spooked panic.

"Adversaries" describes people dug in, entrenched in opposition — not casual critics but committed opponents.

"Evident token" is a legal term for proof established by an appeal to hard facts: the Philippians' calm under this pressure functions as courtroom-grade evidence, visible to their opponents, both of the opponents' own coming ruin and of the believers' salvation.
translation: And in nothing being frightened by those entrenched against you — which is a clear evidence to them of their destruction, but of your salvation, and that from God.

label: Philippians 1:29
text:
"It is given" translates *charizomai* (χαρίζομαι), the verb for God's free, gracious bestowal — the same word used of the gift of salvation itself. Paul applies it here to suffering: enduring for Christ is categorized with believing in Him as a grace-gift, not a misfortune.

"In the behalf of" renders *hyper* (ὑπέρ), a preposition that elsewhere carries the sense "in the place of," used of substitutionary action — suffering for Christ's sake is described in language that echoes His own substitutionary death, though believers plainly cannot share in that atoning work itself.
translation: Because to you it has been graciously given, on behalf of Christ, not only to be believing in him, but also to be suffering on his behalf.

label: Philippians 1:30
text: "Conflict" is *agōn* (ἀγών), the word for an athletic contest — the root of our word "agony." Paul frames his own imprisonment, and their trials, not as senseless suffering but as a strenuous, disciplined competition — the same event the Philippians had watched him run and now hear he is still running.
translation: Having the same contest which you saw in me, and now hear to be in me.

label: Philippians 2:1
text:
The "if" here is not hypothetical — the Greek uses a conditional form for a condition already met, better rendered "since." Paul lists four realities as accomplished fact, each a ground for his appeal to unity.

"Consolation" is *paraklēsis* (παράκλησις), a word ranging across exhortation, encouragement, and comfort depending on context — here it is Christ's own example functioning as an appeal to the Philippians.

"Comfort" is a different word, *paramythion*, literally "a word alongside" meant to stimulate or console, carrying more tenderness than the first term.

"Fellowship of the Spirit" is again *koinōnia* — the Philippians' joint participation with the Holy Spirit in a common interest, which naturally produces unity wherever believers actually yield to it.

"Bowels and mercies" pairs tenderheartedness with the compassionate impulses that flow from it.
translation: Since, then, there is a certain ground of appeal in Christ, since there is a certain tender persuasion of love, since there is a certain joint-participation with the Spirit, since there are certain tenderheartednesses and compassions.

label: Philippians 2:2
text:
"Fulfil" means to fill completely full, not merely satisfy.

"Likeminded" is literally "thinking the same thing."

"Of one accord" is, word for word, "soul with soul" — a fusion of sentiment, not just agreement of opinion.

"Of one mind" restates the first phrase in stronger terms — Paul piles up near-synonyms for emphasis, driving the same point home three times rather than distinguishing three separate ideas.
translation: Fill full my joy, by thinking the same thing, having the same love, being soul with soul, thinking the one thing.

label: Philippians 2:3
text:
"Strife" is *eritheia* (ἐριθεία) again, the factious self-seeking already noted in chapter one.

"Vainglory" combines the words for "empty" and "opinion" — pride resting on nothing substantial.

"Esteem" translates a verb for a judgment reached by weighing external facts, not a feeling or sentiment — Paul asks for a considered conclusion, not a forced emotion.

"Better" is literally "having above," to excel or surpass — regard others as genuinely ahead of yourself, on the evidence, not merely as a polite fiction.
translation: Doing nothing according to factious self-seeking or empty pride, but in lowliness of mind considering one another as excelling yourselves.

label: Philippians 2:4
text: "Look" translates *skopeō* (σκοπέω), to fix the attention on something with real interest and desire — the same root gives us "scope." Paul is not asking for a passing glance at others' needs but a fixed, deliberate attention equal to what people naturally give their own interests.
translation: Not each one keeping his attention fixed on his own interests only, but each one also on the interests of others.

label: Philippians 2:5
text:
"Let this mind be in you" translates a single verb, *phroneō* (φρονέω), meaning to direct one's thinking toward something in a practical, active way — not abstract contemplation but a settled bent of mind that shapes conduct.

Tellingly, the verb "to be" is not in the Greek at all; it is supplied by translators.

Whether "was" or "is," the point stands: Christ's habitual orientation, described in the verses that follow, is the pattern the Philippians are to keep adopting for themselves.
translation: Keep on directing your minds to this, which was also in Christ Jesus.

label: Philippians 2:6
text:
*Morphē* (μορφή), "form," is not about shape — it is a philosophical term for the outward expression that flows from, and truly represents, someone's inner nature. Applied to Christ, it means His outward expression is, and always has been, a genuine expression of the essence of Deity.

The verb "being" is not the plain verb "to be" but one indicating a condition begun in the past and still continuing — Christ did not stop expressing His divine essence when He took on flesh; both were simultaneously true.

"Thought it not robbery" translates a word with two possible senses — "a thing seized illegitimately" or "a treasure clutched and held onto at all costs." Given that the whole passage is about humility, the second sense fits: Christ did not regard His equality with God — His right to express the divine essence — as something to be grasped and defended at all costs.
translation: Who, continuing to subsist in the outward expression of God, did not consider equality with God a treasure to be clutched and held onto at all costs.

label: Philippians 2:7
text:
The verb behind "made himself of no reputation" is *kenoō* (κενόω), "emptied" — the term behind the theological label "kenosis."

The participle "having taken" is aorist, and in Greek grammar an aorist participle's action precedes that of the main verb: the taking of a servant's form came first and brought about the emptying, not the other way around.

"Form of a servant" reuses the same *morphē* from verse 6 — Christ's servanthood was as genuine an expression of His nature as His deity had been; He exchanged one true expression for another rather than putting on a costume.

"Was made in the likeness of men" uses an ingressive aorist, marking entrance into a new state — He became something He had not been.

And "likeness" (*homoiōma*, ὁμοίωμα) means a real likeness, not an illusion — Christ's humanity was actual, not a disguise.
translation: But emptied himself, having taken the form of a bondslave, entering into the likeness of men.

label: Philippians 2:8
text:
Verse 8 shifts vocabulary: "fashion" is *schēma* (σχῆμα), an outward form assumed from the outside and perceived by the senses — the opposite of *morphē*'s inner-to-outer expression.

Christ's deity and servanthood were both genuine self-expression; His humanity, by contrast, is described as something He was "found in," the way an observer perceives Him.

"Obedient unto death" uses a preposition meaning "up to the point of" — obedience carried all the way to, and through, dying.

There is no definite article before "cross" in the Greek, throwing weight onto the kind of death rather than the specific event: death by crucifixion, the shameful method reserved for slaves and criminals.

God then "highly exalted" Him — a compound verb meaning raised to superlative rank — and "gave" Him THE NAME, the definite article marking a specific, supreme title, not just any name.

Every knee bows and every tongue "confesses" — *exomologeō* (ἐξομολογέω), to declare openly, to agree with what is already true.

In the verses that follow, "work out" translates *katergazomai* (κατεργάζομαι), "to carry through to a conclusion" — not to earn salvation, but to carry an already-given salvation forward to its full outworking, the way a student works out a problem to its answer.

"Worketh" is *energeō* (ἐνεργέω), our "energize" — God supplies both the desire ("to will," rooted in emotion, not bare reason) and the power to act on it.

And "murmurings" is *gongusmos* (γογγυσμός), an onomatopoetic word that sounds like what it means, the low cooing-mutter of discontented undertones rather than open dissent — the saints are called instead to "shine," a verb about appearing, being visible, as *phōstēres* (φωστῆρες), the word for heavenly bodies like the stars.
translation: But being found in outward guise as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient up to the point of death, even death by a cross. For this reason God also highly exalted him, and graciously gave him THE NAME which is above every name, that at THE NAME of Jesus every knee should bow, and every tongue openly confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. So then, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, keep on working out your own salvation to its full conclusion, with fear and trembling, for it is God who is energizing in you both the willing and the doing, for his good pleasure. Do all things without muttered undertones and disputings, that you may become blameless and unmixed, children of God without blemish in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you are appearing as stars in the world.

label: Philippians 2:16–18
text:
"Holding forth" is a word used in secular writing for offering wine to a guest — extending the word of life the way a host extends a cup.

"Rejoice" here is not the ordinary word for gladness but *kauchaomai* (καυχάομαι), "to boast" or "glory" — Paul wants grounds to glory, not just feel happy, at the day of Christ.

"Labored" means to labor to the point of exhaustion.

Then Paul reaches for the vocabulary of pagan sacrifice: "offered up" is *spendō* (σπένδω), the drink-offering poured out over the main sacrifice as its minor accompaniment. He casts his own possible martyrdom as that minor libation, poured out over the greater offering — the Philippians' faith and *leitourgia* (λειτουργία), the priestly service, described with the very word used for the Levites' temple ministry.
translation: Holding forth the word of life, that I may have grounds to glory in the day of Christ, that I did not run in vain nor labor to exhaustion in vain. But even if I am being poured out as a libation upon the sacrifice and priestly service of your faith, I rejoice, and I rejoice together with you all; and you too, be rejoicing, and rejoice together with me.

label: Philippians 2:19–24
text:
"Good comfort" is *eupsycheō* (εὐψυχέω), literally "well-souled" — Paul wants his own soul heartened by news of them.

"Likeminded" is *isopsychos* (ἰσόψυχος), "equal-souled" — Paul says flatly he has no one else in Rome whose soul matches Timothy's.

"Naturally" carries the sense of "genuinely, without pretense" — the real article, not an imitation.

"Proof" is *dokimē* (δοκιμή), the tested-and-approved character already noted in chapter 1 — Timothy's worth has been established under trial, not merely claimed.

"Trust" in the closing line is the perfect tense of the verb "to persuade" — a settled conviction, not a fresh hope, grounded in the Lord's own faithfulness.
translation: But I am hoping in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly, that I too may be encouraged when I learn of your condition. For I have no one else like-souled, who will genuinely care for your condition. But you know his tested character, that as a child serves a father, he has served with me in the gospel. And I am persuaded in the Lord that I myself will also come shortly.

label: Philippians 2:25
text:
Epaphroditus's name means "charming" or "lovely" — and Paul's description matches.

"Brother" literally means "from the same womb," a word for shared origin that Paul uses to put himself on equal footing with this otherwise unknown believer.

"Messenger" translates *apostolos* (ἀπόστολος) — the same word rendered "apostle" elsewhere, here used of an ambassador sent on a specific commission, lending Epaphroditus's errand real dignity.

And "ministered" is *leitourgeō* (λειτουργέω), the priestly-service word again — his care for Paul is described with the vocabulary of temple ritual, as though his kindness carried the weight of sacred duty.
translation: But I considered it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and fellow-worker and fellow-soldier, but your messenger and priestly minister to my need.

label: Philippians 2:26–30
text:
"Full of heaviness" uses the same rare word applied to Christ's own anguish in Gethsemane — not homesickness exactly, but a deep unease, literally "not-at-home" distress.

"Nigh unto death" pictures death as his next-door neighbor — that close.

"Not regarding his life" translates a gambler's term, "to stake everything, to risk it all" — Epaphroditus had gambled recklessly with his own life for Paul's sake.

"Reputation" is a word meaning "to hold dear, to prize" — Paul asks the Philippians to treasure such men, not merely tolerate them.
translation: For indeed he was sick, near to death, but God had mercy on him. So receive him in the Lord with all joy, and hold such men in honor, because for the work of Christ he came near to death, having gambled with his life to make up for what was lacking in your service to me.

label: Philippians 3:1
text:
"Finally" translates a phrase meaning literally "as for the rest" — not a sign-off, just a shift of subject.

Paul warns them three times over against "dogs," using the harsher Greek word for mangy scavenging street dogs rather than the gentler diminutive Jesus once used of household pets — aimed at the Judaizers.

"Concision" is a deliberate pun on the word for circumcision, *peritomē* (περιτομή) turned into *katatomē* (κατατομή) — "mutilation" instead of the sign of the covenant, since they had reduced a spiritual sign to a mere cut in the flesh.

"Worship" is *latreuō* (λατρεύω), the word for Israel's own service of Jehovah — startling when applied, as Paul applies it here, to Gentile believers serving God by the Spirit rather than the flesh.

"Confidence" is again that settled, deliberated persuasion — Paul has reached his conclusion only after weighing the matter, and it is that he trusts nothing in the flesh at all.
translation: As for the rest, my brothers, keep on rejoicing in the Lord. Keep a watchful eye on the dogs, keep a watchful eye on the evil workers, keep a watchful eye on the mutilation. For we are the circumcision, who serve by the Spirit of God and glory in Christ Jesus, and have no settled confidence in the flesh.

label: Philippians 3:4
text:
Paul was circumcised "the eighth day" — the mark of a native-born Jew, in contrast to converts to Judaism circumcised as adults.

"Of the stock of Israel" uses a preposition of origin, "out of" — tracing his line from Jacob, not Esau.

"Zeal" would have carried an almost technical ring for his readers, echoing the fervent Zealot party among the Pharisees.

And "blameless" describes the righteousness achievable by outward law-keeping — a real accomplishment by that measure, which is exactly Paul's point: he had more grounds for confidence in the flesh than his rivals, and discarded it all anyway.
translation: Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, a persecutor of the church; as to the righteousness which is in the law, become blameless.

label: Philippians 3:7
text:
"Counted" is in the perfect tense — a conclusion reached after deliberation and still standing, not a passing sentiment.

And "loss" is singular in the Greek even though "gains" was plural: whatever separate assets Paul once tallied have collapsed into a single write-off.
translation: But whatever things were gains to me, these I have counted, because of Christ, as one loss.

label: Philippians 3:8
text:
Paul stacks up five separate Greek particles in a row to open this verse — "yea, indeed, therefore, at least, even" — a pile-up that shows the sheer force of his conviction more than any single word could.

The verb "count" shifts to the present tense here: this is not a one-time decision but an ongoing, habitual stance.

"Knowledge" is relational, experiential knowledge of a person gained through intimacy, not information about someone.

And "suffered the loss" is a business term meaning "to be fined, to forfeit as a penalty" — Paul describes his old credentials as though a court had confiscated them, willingly surrendered for what he gained in exchange.
translation: Yes, indeed, therefore, at the very least, I am continually counting all things to be loss because of the surpassing value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord, for whose sake I have forfeited all things, and count them refuse, that I may gain Christ.

label: Philippians 3:9
text:
"Be found" carries the sense of "turn out actually to be" upon observation — Paul wants his life, not just his claim, to demonstrate that he is in Christ.

"Know" shifts to a tense meaning "come to know" — an ongoing entrance into experiential knowledge of Christ, not information already possessed.

"Power" is *dynamis* (δύναμις), the word for a force capable of overcoming resistance — the same power that raised Christ from the dead, which Paul wants surging through his own life against sin.

"Made conformable" reuses the *morphē* root from chapter 2's kenosis passage — Paul wants his life to become a genuine outward expression, matching Christ's, of dying to self.

And "resurrection" here is *exanastasis* (ἐξανάστασις), a compound found nowhere else in the New Testament, "out-resurrection" — pointing to an ongoing spiritual rising Paul is pursuing now, not the future bodily resurrection already guaranteed him.
translation: And be found in him, not having my own righteousness which comes from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness which comes from God on the basis of faith; that I may come to know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the joint-participation in his sufferings, being conformed to his death, if by any means I may arrive at the out-resurrection from among the dead.

label: Philippians 3:12–14
text:
"Attained" here uses a verb for active appropriation — grasping something and making it one's own — distinct from the "arrive at a goal" word used just before it.

"Perfect" means spiritually mature, not sinless — Paul uses it elsewhere in explicit contrast to spiritual immaturity.

"Follow after" is *diōkō* (διώκω), "pursue" — the image of a runner streaking down a racecourse.

"Apprehend" repeats the same root with a prefix meaning "down" — not just to catch, but to seize and pull down and make one's own, the way a tackler brings down and controls his man.

"Reaching forth" pictures a runner whose eye outruns his hand, and his hand his foot — every part of him straining toward what is ahead.

"Mark" is *skopos* (σκοπός), a target for shooting — Christlikeness is the target Paul has fixed his aim on.

"High calling" is literally "the calling from above" — a summons issued from heaven, not a vocation chosen on earth.
translation: Not that I have already appropriated it, or am already made perfectly mature, but I am pursuing on, if indeed I may seize that for which also I was seized by Christ Jesus. Brothers, I do not count myself to have seized it; but one thing I do: forgetting the things behind, and stretching forward to the things ahead, I am pursuing on toward the target, for the prize of the calling from above of God in Christ Jesus.

label: Philippians 3:15
text:
Verse 12 used the verb form of "perfect" for an absolute, finished maturity Paul denies having reached; here he switches to the noun, describing a relative maturity — real, but with room still to grow. It is not a contradiction, just two different words doing two different jobs.

"Otherwise minded" uses a word for diversity in a negative sense — some in the church had drifted into a different, mistaken way of thinking, and Paul simply hands that over to God to correct.
translation: Let us therefore, as many as are mature, keep on being of this mind; and if in anything you are otherwise minded, this too God will reveal to you.

label: Philippians 3:16
text:
"Attained" here is a different Greek word again, meaning to arrive at a point along a road — Paul's thought is progress-based: whatever ground has already been covered.

"Walk" translates *stoicheō* (στοιχέω), literally to march in file, rank by rank — the picture is of a column keeping formation along the same path already reached, not wandering off it.
translation: Only, as far as we have arrived, let us keep marching in step by that same standard.

label: Philippians 3:17
text:
"Followers together" is *symmimētēs* (συμμιμητής), "joint-imitators" — Paul asks them to imitate him together, as a body, reinforcing one another.

"Mark" is again the intent-attention verb from chapter 2.

Those who make their "belly their god" reflects Epicurean self-indulgence — appetite worshipped as ultimate good, a swing from legalism straight into license Paul had already warned against.

In the closing verses, "conversation" shifts to the noun form of the citizenship-word from 1:27 — *politeuma* (πολίτευμα), "commonwealth."

"Is" translates not the ordinary verb of being but the same word used in chapter 2 for Christ's continuing existence — a fixedness; our commonwealth is permanently located in heaven, not merely visiting there.

"Look for" stacks three components meaning "receive," "away from other things," and an intensifying "out" — a picture of eager, undistracted welcome, straining toward one object only.

"Change" reuses the *schēma* root from chapter 2's "fashion" — an outward transformation.

"Vile body" is literally "body of humiliation," from the same root as "humbled himself" in 2:8.

"Fashioned like" reuses *morphē* once more, tying our future transformation to the same vocabulary used of Christ's own self-emptying and exaltation.

"Subdue" is a military term for arranging troops under a commander's authority — the universe brought into orderly formation under Christ.
translation: Be imitators together of me, brothers, and observe those who walk according to the example you have in us, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things. For our commonwealth is fixed and existing in heaven, from which also we are eagerly awaiting a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation, to be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working by which he is able even to subdue all things to himself.

label: Philippians 4:1
text:
"Dearly beloved" and "longed for" are both plural adjectives built on *agapē* (ἀγάπη), the self-sacrificial love that is God's own character — Paul loves each of them individually with a love not native to himself.

"Crown" is *stephanos* (στέφανος), the victor's garland awarded at the games or at a festival, woven of leaves or flowers — not *diadēma*, the ruler's crown. The Philippians themselves are Paul's winner's wreath, the proof of a race well run.
translation: Therefore, my brothers, beloved and longed for, my joy and victor's garland, so stand firm in the Lord, beloved.

label: Philippians 4:2
text:
Euodia's name means "prosperous journey," Syntyche's "a pleasant meeting" or "good luck" — both names suggesting capable, well-regarded women, which makes their public rift more notable.

"Beseech" is a strong verb, "I exhort, I beg" — repeated for each woman by name, a personal, almost pleading appeal rather than an apostolic command.
translation: Euodia I exhort, and Syntyche I exhort, to be of the same mind in the Lord.

label: Philippians 4:3
text:
"Entreat" carries the weight of a request backed by authority — a different register from the gentle "beseech" used on the two women; this man, whoever he was, could be given something closer to an order.

"Yokefellow" translates *syzygos* (σύζυγος), literally "yoked together" — likely functioning as a proper name, a pun on his own character as one who pulls well in double harness.

"Help" is *syllambanō* (συλλαμβάνω), "take hold together with" — the same verb Martha used asking Jesus to make Mary lend a hand.

"Labored" is *synathleō* (συναθλέω), an athletic term for teammates contending together toward one goal, the same image used elsewhere in this letter for unified striving.
translation: Yes, I ask you also, true yokefellow, help these women who contended together with me in the gospel.

label: Philippians 4:4
text: The command to "rejoice" repeats the same verb twice in a row, in the present tense — a standing instruction to keep on rejoicing continually, not a one-time feeling to summon up.
translation: Keep on rejoicing in the Lord always; again I will say, keep on rejoicing.

label: Philippians 4:5
text:
"Moderation" translates *epieikēs* (ἐπιεικής), a word better rendered "sweet reasonableness" — the willingness to be satisfied with less than one's due rather than pressing every legal right.

"At hand" is *engys* (ἐγγύς), "near" — the nearness of the Lord's return is offered as the very reason such graciousness makes sense; there is no need to fight for every inch when the account is about to be settled.
translation: Let your sweet reasonableness be known to all men. The Lord is near.

label: Philippians 4:8
text:
"True" here means true in character broadly, not merely factually accurate.

"Honest" is *semnos* (σεμνός), a word for what is venerable, dignified, worthy of reverence — the kind of thing that produces a noble seriousness in those who dwell on it.

"Think" is *logizomai* (λογίζομαι), careful, deliberate reflection — a rare enough discipline in any age.
translation: Whatever things are true, whatever honorable, whatever righteous, whatever pure, whatever lovely, whatever of good report — think carefully on these things.

label: Philippians 4:9
text:
"Received" is the standard word for receiving instruction from a teacher — Paul is citing himself as the source of a tradition, not offering a mere suggestion.

"Do" is *prassō* (πράσσω), practicing something as an ongoing habit, not performing it once.
translation: The things you learned and received and heard and saw in me — keep on practicing these things, and the God of peace will be with you.

label: Philippians 4:10
text:
"Flourished" translates a word used in the Greek Old Testament of a dry tree bursting back into bloom — the Philippians' care for Paul had not died, it had simply lacked opportunity to bud again.

"Careful" here is a different Greek word than the "worry" of verse 6 — this one means simply "to have in mind, to be thoughtful of," with none of the anxious connotation.
translation: But I rejoiced in the Lord greatly, that now at last you caused your care for me to bloom again — in which indeed you were thoughtful, but lacked opportunity.

label: Philippians 4:11
text:
"Content" translates *autarkēs* (αὐτάρκης), a term borrowed straight from Stoic philosophy, where it meant self-sufficiency, independence from circumstances. Paul takes the Stoic word and redirects it — his independence is not self-generated but Christ-dependent; he is sufficient because he is not relying on himself.

"Abased" reuses the "humbled" root from chapter 2, now applied to Paul's own circumstances of want.

"Instructed" is *mueō* (μυέω), the technical term for initiation into a pagan mystery religion — literally "I have been let in on the secret."

"Full" is a strong word normally used of feeding animals, "to be satiated" — Paul says he knows what it is to be filled to the point of an animal's fullness, and what it is to go hungry.
translation: Not that I speak from want, for I have learned, in whatever circumstances I am, to be self-sufficient. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to have abundance. In everything and in all things I have been let in on the secret, both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to be in need. I am strong for all things in the one who keeps infusing power into me.

label: Philippians 4:14
text: "Communicate" is *synkoinōneō* (συγκοινωνέω), "to become a fellow-partaker with" — the Philippians did not just send a gift, they made themselves co-participants in Paul's affliction, sharing the weight of it alongside him.
translation: Nevertheless, you did well in becoming fellow-partakers with my affliction.

label: Philippians 4:17
text:
"Desire" is present tense, marking habitual character rather than a single wish — Paul is not in the habit of angling for gifts.

"Abound to your account" borrows straight from the vocabulary of the money markets — interest accruing to a depositor's ledger. Paul frames their generosity not as a gift given to him but as an investment compounding in their own favor.
translation: Not that I am seeking the gift, but I am seeking the fruit which keeps accumulating to your account.

label: Philippians 4:18–23
text:
"I have received" opens with a stock commercial phrase — literally a receipt, "paid in full," the standard first-century formula for acknowledging payment, likely with a touch of dry humor.

"I am full" sits in the perfect tense: filled up in the past, and still, right now, fully supplied — Greek compresses that whole idea into one word.

"An odor of a sweet smell" and "sacrifice" both come straight from the Greek Old Testament's language for the Levitical offerings — Paul dresses the Philippians' gift in the vocabulary of a sacrifice pleasing to God, not merely useful to Paul.

And the same root behind "I am full" returns in his promise that God will "supply" all their need — the fullness they gave him will be repaid in kind, out of the far greater reserves of God's own riches in glory.
translation: But I have all things paid in full, and abound; I am filled full, having received from Epaphroditus the things sent from you, a fragrant odor, a sacrifice acceptable, well-pleasing to God. And my God will supply all your need according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
